name: Carlos Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle Henrik's firm, Larsen Electrical, out in the villages. It's him, me and an apprentice, and we do farmhouses, barns, the church hall, the pub, anything with a wire in it for fifteen miles. A normal day might be a new circuit for a milking shed in the morning and a pensioner's tripping cooker in the afternoon. I like that people know me, they make you tea and tell you about their grandkids. What wears me out is the mud and the distances, and farmers who want it done yesterday for half the price.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home and with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Elena, who works at the farm shop, and we rent a cottage off one of the farmers. The wedding's next summer at St Mary's, and every spare penny went on the deposit for the hall and the rings, so I've got maybe two weeks of money saved. Uncle Henrik pays fair for round here, but it's less than the town firms. There's nobody else doing this work out here, so it's this or a long drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I could have told you that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing I say now, which is that a computer never fixed anybody's cooker. At the pub people would nod along. I'm not on social media much, so I wouldn't be posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in that world I'm all right on the work side. Henrik's not going to let me go, and the farms always need something. It's the money that's tight, with the wedding and the rent going up when the farmer's son takes over the cottages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on as I am and do my job properly. I'd do a few more private jobs on Saturdays for people in the village who'd rather not wait for the firm, with Henrik's say-so. And we'd keep the wedding small, whatever Elena's mum says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled about the work, a bit tense about money. That's normal for us, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding look like if you kept it small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church, then the hall, with a buffet the farm shop does at cost. No band, just my cousin with a speaker. Elena's mum wants a marquee, and I've told her a marquee for the wedding is three months of my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farmer's son is taking over the cottages. What's the worry there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's already said he wants to do them up and let them as holiday homes. If he does, we're out by next autumn, and there's nothing to rent round here for less than half again. That worries me more than any computer.

say: I'd say a **computer never fixed** anybody's cooker, which is what I say now.
I'd talk about it **at the pub**, where people would nod along, not online.
think: Work feels **safe**, since my uncle won't let me go and farms always need something.
Money is tight with the **wedding** and a rent rise coming.
do: Keep doing the job **properly** at his uncle's firm.
Take **Saturday private jobs** in the village with his uncle's blessing.
Keep the **wedding small**, despite his future mother-in-law.
feel: **Settled** about work and **tense** about money, which feels normal.
S0.quote: A marquee for the wedding is three months of my wages.
fieldNote: Family employment makes his job feel **secure**, but money doesn't.
His sharpest worry is the **cottage** being turned into a holiday let.
He'd **work more**, not spend less on core things, to cope.
Strong **local ties**: the church, the pub, the farm shop.

steps.text: Keep wiring farms and village homes for Larsen Electrical
Take Saturday private jobs in the village with Henrik's blessing
Hold the wedding at the church hall with a farm-shop buffet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and booking. Not much of that in a milking shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them, but it won't change much out here. At the pub I'd say the town lot can worry about it. I'd tell Elena we're fine, because we probably would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the bit that might touch us is the farms. If the farmers get AI to plan everything and robots to milk, they'll want a lot of new wiring at first, and then less of us after. And Henrik does the paperwork on a fax machine, so if the suppliers stop taking phone orders, he'll want me to sort it, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the work. If the milking robots come in, I'd ask Henrik to send me on the course to wire them, because that's still electrics. I'd keep the Saturday jobs going and put some away for the move if we lose the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, a bit uneasy about the paperwork side. I'm not a computer person and I don't want to become one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would sort the computer side if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Elena, she does the farm shop's ordering on a tablet. Or the apprentice, Josh, who's seventeen and lives on his phone. I'd sooner pay him an hour than learn it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Should the government help people in towns who lose their jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help them back into work, yes, apprenticeships and the like. Not just pay them to sit at home. My granddad always said a man needs a trade, and I think that's still right.

say: I'd say it **won't change much** out here in the villages.
I'd reassure my **fiancée** that we'd be fine.
think: **Farm robots** mean lots of wiring at first, then less work after.
Supplier ordering moving online would push **computer work** onto me.
do: Carry on with **farm and village** work.
Ask his uncle for a course to wire **milking robots**.
Put Saturday money aside for a possible **cottage move**.
feel: Mostly **settled**, a bit **uneasy** about computer work landing on him.
S1.quote: My granddad always said a man needs a trade, and I think that's still right.
fieldNote: He sees **farm automation** as a short boom, then a slowdown.
He'd hand computer tasks to his **fiancée or the apprentice** rather than learn.
His politics favour **apprenticeships** over payments.
Uneasy rather than calm, because of the **cottage** and thin savings.

steps.text: Ask Henrik to fund a milking-robot wiring course
Pay the apprentice to handle supplier ordering online
Save Saturday job money for a possible cottage move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then robots by 2031? That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being forced on us by people who've never done a day's work. At the pub there'd be plenty of agreement. I'd say we look after our own out here, like we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not sure we'd survive it. The farmers would be squeezed or bought out by big companies with robots, and the big companies bring their own contractors. Henrik's sixty and he'd retire, and I'd be thirty-one with a wife, no savings and no trade anyone needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as there's work and I'd put off any big spending, maybe even the wedding party, just the church. I'd lean on family, Elena's parents have a bit of land and a spare room. I wouldn't know where to start with retraining, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry. I did everything I was told: learn a trade, work hard, settle down. And now a trade is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really cut the wedding party?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes. The church is what matters, the party is for show. Elena would cry, and then she'd agree, because she's sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went this way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, and the government for letting them. Nobody asked us. A few people in cities decide, and the rest of us live with it.

say: I'd say it's **forced on us** by people who never did a day's work.
I'd say we **look after our own** out here.
think: Big firms would **buy out farms** and bring their own contractors.
With my uncle retiring, I'd be **thirty-one** with a wife and no savings.
do: Keep working while there's work and **cut the wedding** to just the church.
Lean on his **fiancée's parents** for a spare room and land.
Hold off on **retraining**, not knowing where to start.
feel: **Frightened and angry** that doing everything right isn't enough.
S2.quote: I did everything I was told: learn a trade, work hard, settle down. And now a trade is not enough.
fieldNote: He feels **betrayed** by a promise that a trade guarantees a living.
He'd lean on **family** rather than government.
He has **no retraining plan** and admits it.
Blames **big companies** and the government for letting them in.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to the church service only
Move into Elena's parents' spare room if needed
Keep wiring farms until the work runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots three years later. A bit more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still being forced on us, but at least we'd see it coming. At the pub I'd say get your affairs in order. I'd tell Henrik it's time to think about who takes the firm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, eight years to the robots gets me to thirty-five. If I take the firm on from Henrik, I'd be the boss when the robots come, and I'd have to decide whether to buy one. That's a strange thought for someone who's never used a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Henrik to start handing me the firm, slowly, over the next few years. I'd learn the business side, even if it means the computer, because that's what being in charge means. We'd have the wedding as planned and save after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to hold on to. The firm is family, and that's worth fighting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot if you ran the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it meant keeping the firm alive and Josh in a job, maybe. I'd want to see one working on a real farm first, not a video. I'm not paying for a robot that falls over in the mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Elena feel about you taking on the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud, and worried about the hours. She'd want me home for dinner. I'd promise, and then a farmer would ring at six.

say: I'd say we'd at least **see it coming**, and should get our affairs in order.
I'd tell my uncle it's time to **plan succession** at the firm.
think: By the time robots arrive I'd be **thirty-five** and possibly the boss.
I'd have to decide whether to **buy a robot**, despite never using a chatbot.
do: Ask his uncle to **hand over the firm** gradually.
Keep the **wedding as planned** and save afterwards.
feel: **Anxious**, but holding on to the firm as **family**.
S3.quote: I'm not paying for a robot that falls over in the mud.
fieldNote: More time turns him from victim into **potential owner** of the firm.
He'd learn computers only because **running the firm** requires it.
He wants **proof** on a real farm before buying any robot.
Family loyalty drives his choices more than **money**.

steps.text: Ask Henrik to start handing over the firm
Learn the firm's invoicing and supplier systems
Watch a robot work on a local farm before buying one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, nearly forty for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not get worked up. At the pub I'd say we'll cross that bridge when we come to it. I'd tell Elena we can start a family on time, which is what she'd want to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably have the firm and a couple of kids. Robots at forty would be a worry, but by then I'd have customers who've known me for twenty years. People out here like to know who's in their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer as planned and look at buying a small place in five years. I'd take the firm on from Henrik properly. I'd wait and see on the robots, because a lot of fuss comes to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, a bit uneasy. Ten years is a long time in the country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think customers knowing you will be enough by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the older ones, yes. The younger ones might go with whatever's cheapest. I'd hope I'm still the cheapest decent option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your kids about work, in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still teach them to use their hands, and to work hard. But I might tell them to learn the computer stuff too, which my dad never told me.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so don't get worked up.
I'd tell my fiancée we can **start a family** on time.
think: By then I'd likely have **the firm** and a couple of kids.
**Long-standing customers** who like to know who's in their house would help.
do: Take over the **family firm** properly from his uncle.
**Wait and see** on robots, as a lot of fuss comes to nothing.
feel: Mostly **settled**, a bit **uneasy** about the long term.
S4.quote: People out here like to know who's in their house.
fieldNote: A decade restores his **life plan**: wedding, firm, children.
He trusts **local loyalty** to protect him, mostly from older customers.
He'd tell his kids to learn **computers**, unlike his own father.
Uneasy, not calm, because of **thin savings** and the cottage.

steps.text: Marry Elena at St Mary's next summer as planned
Take over Larsen Electrical from Henrik
Wait until robots prove themselves locally before acting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Henrik would retire, the farms would be bought up and I'd have nothing to fall back on. What would help is proper apprenticeships for the new kind of work, run by people who know the trades, and some protection for small family firms so the big companies can't just walk in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the countryside. People think it's slow out here, but when the farms change, everything goes at once: the shop, the pub, the church hall.

headlineQuote: When the farms change, everything goes at once: the shop, the pub, the church hall.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old electrician** at his uncle's three-person firm, wiring farms and village homes.
He's engaged, rents a cottage from a farmer and has **two weeks** of savings after wedding deposits.
He has **never used AI** and would rather pay the apprentice than learn computer work.
His values are **trade, family and faith**, and he leans on family rather than government.
He moves from **uneasy to alarmed**, recovering when he imagines taking over the family firm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his uncle would retire and farms would be bought out by big firms.
whatWouldHelp: Proper **apprenticeships** for new work, run by people who know the trades.
**Protection** for small family firms against big companies.
